n: Job responds to Eliphaz. Instead of arguing theology, he first asks his friends to understand how much he hurts.

f.g: Job replies to Eliphaz’s speech in chapters 4–5.

n: If only someone could weigh my grief and my disaster on a scale!

f.g: Thoroughly.
A set of scales for weighing.

n: His sorrow would outweigh all the sand of the sea — that’s why his words have been wild. Job admits his speech was rash, but asks them to understand why.

f.g: My words have been rash or reckless.

f.w: heavier than the sand of the sea

n: Job feels that God Himself has shot poisoned arrows into him, and terrors from God are lined up against him like an army. He doesn’t know about the heavenly scene in chapters 1–2.

f.g: Line up for battle.

n: Animals don’t complain when they have food. Job’s point: he wouldn’t be crying out if he weren’t truly suffering.

f.g: Moos.
Animal feed.

n: Who can eat bland food without salt, or enjoy the taste of egg white? Eliphaz’s advice tastes just as flat to Job.

f.g: Tasteless.
The Hebrew is uncertain; some think it means the juice of a bland plant.

n: What he once refused to touch has become his miserable diet — his suffering, or perhaps his friends’ counsel, makes him sick.

f.g: Food.

n: Job has one request he longs for God to grant.

f.w: Oh that I might have my request
f.g: A deep wish, often introduced this way in Job.

n: His wish is that God would just end his life — cut the thread of his life like a weaver cuts cloth from the loom.

f.g: Literally cut off like thread from a loom (compare Isaiah 38:12).

n: That would still be a comfort: he could leap for joy even in pain, knowing he never denied the words of the Holy One. Job holds on to his integrity.

f.g: Possibly “leap for joy” or “exult” — the Hebrew is uncertain.

f.w: I have not concealed the words of the Holy One
f.g: I have not denied or rejected God’s words.

n: Job feels he has no strength left to keep hoping and no future worth waiting for.

f.g: What future do I have?

n: He is not made of stone or bronze. Human endurance has limits.

f.g: Bronze.

n: He feels he has no inner resources left; any success has been driven away from him.

f.g: Here possibly “success” or “resourcefulness.”

n: A suffering person should receive loyal kindness from a friend — even if he were to abandon the fear of God. Friendship should not depend on agreement.

f.g: Hebrew hesed — loyal, steadfast kindness.

f.w: To him that is afflicted pity should be shewed

n: Job compares his friends to desert streams: full when there’s no need, dry when you need water. Their friendship has proven unreliable.

f.g: Like a wadi — a seasonal stream that disappears in summer.

n: In winter these streams run dark with melting ice and snow.

f.g: Dark, murky.

n: But when the heat comes, they vanish. When travelers most need them, they are gone.
Caravans turn off their route to find water, but the stream has disappeared, and they wander into the desert and die.

f.w: The paths of their way are turned aside
f.g: Caravans leave the road looking for water.

n: Caravans from Tema and Sheba, Arabian trading peoples, look hopefully for the water.

f.g: An oasis town in northwest Arabia.
A trading kingdom in southern Arabia.

n: Their hopes are crushed; they arrive to find nothing and are put to shame.

f.g: Bewildered, disappointed.

n: So it is with you, Job says: you see my horrible condition and pull back in fear. Perhaps they feared that whatever struck Job could strike them.

f.w: ye see my casting down, and are afraid
f.g: You see my disaster and draw back in fear.

n: Did I ask you for money or gifts? Job had asked nothing of them except understanding.

f.g: Wealth.

n: Did I ask you to rescue me from enemies or pay a ransom? No — only for compassion.

f.g: Buy back, ransom.

n: Job challenges them honestly: Teach me and I’ll be quiet. Show me where I went wrong.

f.w: cause me to understand wherein I have erred

n: Honest words are powerful — but your arguments prove nothing.

f.g: How painful (or how powerful) honest words can be.
Correct, prove wrong.

n: Do you mean to criticize my words? A desperate man’s words are like the wind — don’t hold them against him.

f.g: Empty, passing — not to be taken too seriously.

n: You would even gamble over an orphan and sell out your friend. Job feels betrayed.

f.g: Literally “cast lots over the orphan” — treat the helpless heartlessly.

f.w: dig a pit for your friend
f.g: Possibly “bargain over your friend.”

n: Look me in the face — would I lie to you? Job pleads to be heard as a person, not as a theological case.

f.g: Be willing; please.

n: Turn back and reconsider — don’t be unjust. My integrity is still at stake.

f.g: Change your mind, reconsider.
My innocence is on the line.

n: Is there anything false in my words? Can’t I tell right from wrong? Job insists his conscience is clear.

f.w: cannot my taste discern perverse things?
f.g: Can’t I tell what is evil or wrong?
